title: Everyone studies
hook: every Jew must study, rich or poor, healthy or sick, young or old

segments.voice: Yesterday, the physician, and your line: moderation. What did you take down a notch? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

Who is excused? That's the question behind today's law. Surely the person who is too poor, who spends every hour finding bread. Surely the one who is sick. Surely the old man whose strength is gone, or the father with a family to feed. Maimonides goes down the list, one by one, in his laws of Torah study, and his answer to each of them is the same. Not excused.
screen: `WHO IS EXCUSED?` → `THE POOR? THE SICK? THE OLD?` → `NOT EXCUSED.`

segments.voice: Everyone studies. Here is the law, in plain English. Every man of Israel is obligated to study Torah, whether poor or rich, healthy or suffering, young or very old and weak. Even a poor man who lives on charity and goes door to door. Even a man with a wife and children. He must set a fixed time to study, by day and by night, because the verse says: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Turn it four ways. First, the list. Maimonides names exactly the people anyone would excuse, and refuses to excuse them. Study is not a hobby for people with spare time. Second, the fixed time. He doesn't ask for hours. He asks for a set time, kept. A little, on purpose, regularly, is how a busy life holds learning. Third, the examples. In the next law he says that among the great sages of Israel were woodcutters and water carriers, and some were blind, and still they studied day and night. The giants of the tradition were not all people of leisure. Fourth, how long. Until when must a person study? Until the day of death. Learning has no graduation. Now, honestly: Maimonides writes this as a duty of men. A little later he says a woman who studies Torah receives reward, but he does not make it her obligation, and he adds cautions. Jewish communities read this differently today. Some keep the obligation as Maimonides framed it, while also teaching women Torah seriously; others hold women and men to the same duty to learn. Across those differences, the core of the law still lands: being too busy, too poor or too old is not the end of learning.
screen: `RICH OR POOR, SICK OR WELL.` · `A FIXED TIME, KEPT.` · `WOODCUTTERS AND WATER CARRIERS.` · `UNTIL THE DAY OF DEATH.` · then, large: `THOU SHALT MEDITATE THEREIN DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to study for five minutes. The bell gives you two of them now. Choose one short text you have nearby: a verse, a line from Pirkei Avot, a paragraph of anything that teaches. Read it once, slowly. Read it again, and notice one word you'd want to ask about. Then close your eyes and turn that word over. After the bell, give it three more minutes, today. A small, fixed time. The bell holds the time.
Everyone studies. Maimonides' law that Torah study belongs to rich and poor, healthy and sick, young and old, with a fixed time, until the end of life. Today's word.
Your line: everyone studies. Today, pick a time, even five minutes, and give it to learning something, on purpose, no matter how busy the day gets. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition encourages fixed times for Torah study, alone, with a study partner, or in a class at synagogue, and some Jews follow a daily study cycle so that a little is learned every day.

what a scholar hears: Hilkhot Talmud Torah 1:8–10, written as an obligation on men, with 1:13 on women, and read differently across today's movements.
